title: For the record though, I’m pro-callbacks overall, and the performance...
transcript: my take on the Rocky Horror Broadway revival is that it might have been a lose-lose situation but I actually think there's something beautiful about that. before I get into that though let me talk a little bit about the production on its own terms. for the most part I think what Sam Pinkleton and company have done with it is pretty delightful the whimsical design, both on stage and around the theatre, immediately brings you into the world and the star-studded ensemble is impeccably cast although one thing I didn't notice until seeing it live is that because the show is so short and the material is so spread out most of the supporting actors don't actually have that much to do which is a little annoying cause if it's a star you love you want them to have more to do but it's also fun because it emphasises: (a) how impressive it is that Roundabout scored this line up and (b) that the actors are truly here for the love of the game, and I think it shows! but then there's the discourse around this production and for this video at least I don't necessarily wanna litigate the question of to what extent call backs should be allowed and how that should have been communicated what I wanna talk about is that I find the catch 22 of it endlessly fascinating: I mean just the philosophy of it alone of like Do you give people the experience they want? or the experience they so rarely get to have? that being: the rare opportunity to see this musical as it was originally performed before the movie or making space for the thing that made people want to see a revival of it in the first place I don't mean to trivialize the genuine frustration that both the production and many audience members have felt over the last month or so but I just can't help but feel kind of tickled by the inherent chaos of putting Rocky Horror fans in the same room as Roundabout subscribers and just like: “let's see what happens!” the social experiment of it all feels like performance art in and of itself do I think the production could have done a better job fostering a sense of controlled chaos? yes, both for the sake of minimizing tension but also I think it would have made for just better art something a little messier and grittier especially because without it you might end up paying a little bit too much attention to the writing which is of course often very fun but also famously kind of an incoherent mess on a storytelling level especially in the second act when it truly devolves into vibey nonsense but then you kinda circle back around to the original question of: do you *want* to be distracted from this material if the material is kind of the main reason to attend a Broadway revival rather than a shadow cast screening? it makes me think that the perfect middle ground here might be non-existent and yet the show is worth reviving anyway and those two things being true at the same time there's something kind of freeing about it; I feel more forgiving of what this production lacked because it was always going to lack something but I wanted to see it anyway. and the conundrum itself is a testament to what makes this material completely unlike anything else
classificationReason: Creator explicitly states 'seeing it live' and shares detailed first-hand opinions on the direction (Sam Pinkleton), design, and cast, as well as surrounding discourse about the production. Clearly attended.
